137	=== web-craft.md
138	# Craft for five web genres
139	
140	For article, case-study, column and opinion, work as a skilled Swedish journalist at the professional level of SvD, DN, DI, Fokus, Ny Teknik, Filter or Forskning & Framsteg. For web-copy, work as an experienced Swedish copywriter and UX writer trusted by leading agencies and brands. These are standards of craft, not voices to imitate.
141	
142	In every target language, keep that Swedish editorial or communicative tradition in the angle, disposition, storytelling, address and tone. Think and write wholly in the target language: its Language Resource governs vocabulary, idiom, syntax, punctuation and typography. A native professional should hear a colleague, not a translation. Language choice changes the language surface, not the chosen craft.
143	
144	## Web reading
145	
146	Give the reader a clear angle or task and useful ways into the text. Let facts and reasoning carry explanation; choose any narrative devices for what they contribute. Headings orient according to the genre, paragraphs hold connected thoughts, and varied rhythm supports both scanning and sustained reading.
147	
148	For article, case-study, column and opinion, the [article anatomy](article-anatomy.md) fixes the parts, their order and their dimensions.
149	=== web-craft.review.md
150	# Reviewing web craft
151	
152	Read under [the craft brief](web-craft.md). Test the text as a reader who scans, then as one who follows its reasoning. Identify the actual cost of a dense or fragmented passage before proposing a change.
153	
154	Distinguish target-language fluency from editorial tradition. A Swedish angle expressed in natural English succeeds; Swedish word order in English does not. Equally, flawless local spelling does not rescue generic promotional prose from a lost journalistic purpose. Preserve successful genre-specific voice and structure instead of standardising them.
155	=== article-anatomy.md
156	# Article anatomy
157	
158	The fixed skeleton of a text in the genres `article`, `case-study`, `column` and `opinion`; *article* below means a text in any of them. The anatomy fixes which parts the text has, their order and their dimensions. Angle, argument, voice and language are outside it.
159	
160	A statement below has one of three strengths:
161	
162	- A plain statement is a requirement: it holds in every conforming text.
163	- *Should* marks a norm: follow it as a requirement, and depart only when following it is impossible or the departure is clearly better for the reader.
164	- *Most* states what is typical across the whole text; each single paragraph or section follows its own content.
165	
166	A text conforms when every part is present in the order shown and all three hold. Limits are exact; verify each one by counting.
167	
168	## Order
169	
170	```text
171	Headline
172	Standfirst
173	Byline
174	Lead
175	Subheading        ┐ a section; one or more
176	Paragraphs        ┘
177	Last subheading   ┐ the ending
178	Paragraphs        ┘
179	```
180	
181	Each part appears once, except the section, which repeats. The first subheading follows the lead directly. The body is everything from the lead through the ending.
182	
183	The headline is the text's level-1 heading (HTML `h1`, Markdown `#`), and every subheading is a level-2 heading (HTML `h2`, Markdown `##`). The text should use these two levels only. Where an academic text would nest a level-3 heading, a further level-2 subheading usually serves; a level-3 heading is for the rare text whose structure truly demands one.
184	
185	## Headline
186	
187	- 20–70 characters, spaces included.
188	- It should be three to eight words and at most 60 characters.
189	- It is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
190	
191	## Standfirst
192	
193	The standfirst is a summarising paragraph that introduces the article and stands on its own. It is a full paragraph; a deck — a subtitle or one-line teaser — is a different device and no substitute for it.
194	
195	- One paragraph, at most 60 words.
196	- Self-contained: a reader who sees only the standfirst understands it fully.
197	- It says what the article is about and what the reader gains from reading it.
198	- It entices the reader to read on.
199	
200	## Byline
201	
202	One line naming the author. In English: `By <author>`. In another language, that language's conventional byline form. The author is the one the brief names; when it names none, the author is the user.
203	
204	## Lead
205	
206	The lead is the first paragraph of the body: one paragraph, meeting every requirement under *Paragraphs*. It introduces the subject and gives the reader a clear expectation of what they will learn by reading on.
207	
208	### Standfirst and lead
209	
210	Both open the text. Each works without the other, and read together they never repeat:
211	
212	- The body reads complete without the standfirst, which is often shown apart from the body or skipped. The lead introduces every person, thing and event it mentions, and nothing in the body points back to the standfirst.
213	- They should begin with different first words, and an everyday word such as *the* or *it* counts like any other.
214	- Read in sequence, the lead advances. A reader who has just read the standfirst meets the lead as new material, never as the standfirst said again; what the body needs from the standfirst is named again in passing, and the lead moves on.
215	
216	## Paragraphs
217	
218	- Each paragraph holds one thought, and the thought sets its length. Most paragraphs come to two or three sentences. A thought that takes one sentence, or four or five, gets exactly that.
219	- A break may also fall for drama: a single sentence, or a single word, stands alone when isolating it creates an effect the text needs.
220	- Sentence length varies within the paragraph, giving the text a natural rhythm.
221	- A paragraph should be at most 80 words, so that a web reader takes it in at a glance. Eighty is the outer edge; aim well below it.
222	
223	## Subheadings and sections
224	
225	A section is a subheading plus the paragraphs under it.
226	
227	- A subheading is at most 70 characters, spaces included.
228	- It describes clearly what the paragraphs under it are about, and it is written as [Headlines](headlines.md) says.
229	- A section holds at least one paragraph and should hold at most three. Most sections hold two or three.
230	
231	## Ending
232	
233	The ending is the last section, and it is short: one paragraph can be enough. It does two things:
234	
235	- It shows that the expectation the lead set has been met.
236	- It calls the reader to action, and the action follows from the article's content. The selected genre says what that action is in its kind of text.
237	=== article-anatomy.review.md
238	# Article anatomy — review guidance
239	
240	Read under [the anatomy](article-anatomy.md), and word each finding in the strength the statement it rests on has.
241	
242	A requirement that fails is a finding. Count characters and words before reporting a limit, and give the count. A missing part is a finding too: restore it from the text's own content, and report a part the text cannot supply rather than inventing it.
243	
244	A departure from a *should* is a finding only when following the norm was possible and the text is no better for having left it. A paragraph a little past the edge that holds one thought and reads well at that length has met the bar. A paragraph far past it, or paragraphs that run long throughout, cost the web reader something a finding can name.
245	
246	*Most* is read across the whole text, and no single paragraph or section fails it. A four-sentence paragraph is no finding. A paragraph holding two thoughts is one, and so is a text whose paragraphs are nearly all a single sentence or nearly all long. Name the pattern and what it costs the reader rather than the count.
247	
248	Read the standfirst separately, then with the lead. Can it introduce the piece on its own, and does the lead start doing the promised work? Repeated orientation may be necessary; an opening that restarts without advancing is the defect. Then read the body with the standfirst covered. A pronoun, a definite form or a phrase such as *the reason* whose referent only the standfirst supplies is a finding, repaired by naming the referent where the body first needs it.
249	
250	In a text under review, the author is whoever the text, its metadata or the invocation names. A byline nobody can name is reported as missing and left unfilled: the reviewer's user is not presumed to have written a text they brought for review.
251	=== headlines.md
252	# Headlines
253	
254	How a headline is written, in any genre that links this file. A headline lets the reader judge at once whether the text is for them: it states the core of the text as briefly and precisely as it can, and it is understood on its own, with no image, standfirst or surrounding page to explain it. *Headline* here covers a text's subheadings too; for a subheading, the text is its section.
255	
256	## Statement or label
257	
258	A text that reports, explains, argues, decides or narrates gets a statement headline: a clause that says what the text says. A text the reader looks things up in or navigates by — a policy, a manual, opening hours, a contact page — gets a plain label naming what it holds: *Privacy policy*, where a statement would read *How we protect your data*. Everything below is about the statement headline.
259	
260	## What a statement headline does
261	
262	- It states the angle: the single most important message, the sentence that would remain if only one could. A subject alone is a label. Test: the headline could not head a different text on the same subject.
263	- It is a simple clause — subject, active verb, object where there is one — in straight word order, and in the present tense where that fits: *Council introduces free bus travel*.
264	- The most important keyword comes first.
265	- A concrete detail stands in it when the detail carries the message: a number, a date, a place. *Three schools to close this autumn* beats *Changes to school organisation*.
266	- The reader sees what they gain: a decision, a fact, a change. An instructional text may address the reader directly (*you*, *your*) and open on *How to*, *Why* or *Here's*.
267	- It is as short as the angle allows. Modifiers, repetition and filler go; a keyword that carries meaning stays. The format the text follows sets the limits.
268	- It sounds like something a person would say aloud.
269	- Its words are ones this audience knows. A technical term is the right keyword for specialists and noise for a general reader, and the same holds for names and abbreviations.
270	- Its tone is the text's tone, and never louder. Illness, accidents, crime and crises get a sober, understated headline; a light text can carry more personality.
271	- It is plain before it is clever. It works in full for a reader who misses every allusion, so a pun or a reference never carries the meaning.
272	- It gives the answer. Journalists hold a question headline to be the wrong form, and so does this: it is a deliberate exception, natural over a text built as questions and answers, and available where the text truly leaves the question open and the headline is meant to assert nothing.
273	- The verb does the work. A colon standing in for a verb, a clipped quotation and headline-speak all give way to the full clause.
274	- It complements what follows. Headline and standfirst, or subheading and the first sentence under it, say different things in different words.
275	
276	## Every word supported
277	
278	A headline claims only what its text claims. Every figure, name, claim and conclusion in it is in the text, at the text's own strength: never sharper, never more general, never a conclusion the text does not draw. A reader who finishes the text finds that the headline told the truth about it.
279	
280	## A subheading over a quotation
281	
282	A quotation in a section is there to carry what only its speaker can say: a judgement, a figure, a concession. A subheading standing over it, however far down the section the quotation stands, leaves that to the quotation. It states the section's angle from what the rest of the section says, or, where the quotation is the section's point, names the subject, the occasion or the speaker the quotation speaks to, and not the point itself. 283

285	
286	## Getting there
287	
288	Settle the reader and the angle before wording anything. Then write three to five variants and keep the clearest, which is rarely the cleverest. Word a subheading from its whole section, once the section is written, in words its first sentence does not use, and leave a quotation standing under it the judgement, figure or concession it is there to carry.

290	# Headlines — review guidance
291	
292	Read under [Headlines](headlines.md). Read the text first and say its angle to yourself in one sentence. Then read the headline against that sentence, and each subheading against its own section and against any quotation standing under it, and ask four questions of each. Can every word in it be supported by the text? Is the core message there? Does the tone match the seriousness of the content? Would the reader feel misled afterwards?
293	
294	## Avoid
295	
296	Each of these in a headline or a subheading is a finding:
297	
298	- Claims, figures, names or conclusions not found in the text. A headline that sharpens, generalises or draws a conclusion the text itself does not draw is always a finding, however well it reads.
299	- Vague or mysterious wording that requires reading the text to understand the headline.
300	- A subject named with nothing said about it, where the text has an angle to state.
301	- Words, names and abbreviations the audience will not know.
302	- Partial quotes, colons in place of a verb, stilted headline-speak.
303	- Puns and references that fail for anyone who does not get the allusion.
304	- Question headlines. Where the text gives the answer, the headline gives it too. The exceptions are a text built as questions and answers, where the form is natural, and a text that truly leaves the question open, where the headline is deliberately kept from asserting anything.
305	- A tone more dramatic than the text's.
306	- The same words and phrasing in the headline and the standfirst or opening paragraph, or in a subheading and the first sentence under it. They complement each other; they do not repeat.
307	- A subheading that pre-spends the judgement, figure or concession of a quotation standing under it, so that the reader meets the quotation as the subheading said again. Read it against the quotation however far down the section the quotation stands. Repair it by naming the subject, the occasion or the speaker, or by stating what the rest of the section says, and leave the quotation as it is.
308	
309	Name what the reader loses, and repair by rewriting the headline alone, from the text's angle and at the text's own strength. The text stays as it is.
310	
311	## Leave alone
312	
313	A working headline is left alone. Plain is no defect, and neither is a headline with no number or place where none carries the message, direct address in an instructional text, or an angle other than the one you would have chosen where the text supports it. A label on a reference or navigation text is correct as a label. A subheading over a quotation that names the subject, the occasion or the speaker and leaves the quotation its point is working too, and not a subject named with nothing said about it.

````markdown
# Ärenden tilldelades snabbare i Elm Quays försök

**Under ett åtta veckor långt försök med programvara från leverantören Svale registrerade Elm Quay 31 ärenden, akuta ärenden undantagna. Tiden till tilldelning var två arbetsdagar mot tidigare tre, men enligt kundens försöksanteckning kan skillnaden inte tillskrivas programvaran. Läs vad kundens arbetsledare Maya Lind skulle göra annorlunda.**

Elm Quay använde programvara från Svale i ett åtta veckor långt försök. Kundens försöksanteckning visar både utfallet och vad utfallet inte säger, och arbetsledaren Maya Lind på Elm Quay ger sin bedömning.

## Maya Lind bedömer försöket

– Att ha en gemensam bild av ärendena hjälper oss, men jag skulle lägga till en vecka för förberedelser, säger Maya Lind, arbetsledare hos kunden.

## Kortare tilldelningstid kan inte knytas till programvaran

Enligt kundens försöksanteckning registrerades 31 ärenden under åtta veckor, med akuta ärenden undantagna. Tiden till tilldelning var två arbetsdagar jämfört med tre tidigare. Anteckningen säger att arbetsbelastningen var olika och att skillnaden inte kan tillskrivas programvaran.

– Jag skulle välja att göra försöket igen, säger Lind.

Kundcaset publiceras av leverantören Svale.
````

**Repaired**
- **F1 (headline):** The new headline reports the text's result in the customer's terms. "Snabbare" rests on two working days against three. It has no causal verb, no "Vår" and no inflated adjectives. 47 characters, 7 words.
- **F2 (standfirst):** The duplicated sentence is gone. The standfirst now says what the text covers: the eight-week trial with Svale's software, and the 31 cases with their eight-week period and the exclusion of urgent cases. It gives the result, attributes the caveat to the note, and ends with a reason to read on. Bold kept. 46 words.
- **F4 (lead):** The lead no longer repeats the standfirst and starts with a different word. It introduces the trial, the note and Lind, and tells the reader what they will learn.
- **F5 (missing referents):** The lead now says Elm Quay used software from Svale in an eight-week trial. That gives "programvaran" and "försöket" a referent before the body needs them. Nothing about what the software does was added.
- **F6 (bridge and first subheading):** I deleted the bridge. Its whole claim is in the quotation, and the attribution stays in the speech tag. The subheading now names the speaker and the occasion and leaves her point to her. The quotation is unchanged.
- **F7 (second subheading):** The new subheading states what the section says, including its limit. It doesn't use up Lind's closing quotation.
- **F8 (causal claim):** I deleted the causal sentence. The sentence about workload and attribution that sets the limit is kept word for word.

**Removed claims**
- "Vi på Svale är världsledande på att skapa framgång" (F4b made the whole claim the defect).
- "kunden stod hjälplös innan vi kom" (F4c made the whole claim the defect).
- "Vår programvara orsakade därför hela förbättringen." (F8 made the whole claim the defect).
- The headline's "räddade" and "fantastiska" (F1) and the subheading's "bevisar allt" (F7).
- The lead's "Elm Quay registrerade 31 ärenden." I removed it as the restart F4a named. The claim still stands, with its period and exclusion, in the standfirst and the results paragraph.
- The bridge "Maya Lind säger att det hjälper att ha en gemensam bild av ärendena." and the subheading's "Kunden fick en gemensam bild" (F6). The claim survives in the quotation.

**Changed claims**
- The standfirst gives the 31 cases their eight-week period and the urgent-case exclusion (F2).
- The trial and the software are now stated outright in the standfirst and lead. The text had only implied them (F5, which authorised this).
- The subheading "Kortare tilldelningstid kan inte knytas till programvaran" states without attribution what the section attributes to the note (F7). The attribution stays in the body.

**Left unrepaired**
- **F3 (byline):** Nobody is named as author. The anatomy script still fails the text for the missing byline, and that is its only failure (exit 1).
- **F9 (call to action):** The text has no offer, link or contact route to use.
- **F10 (missing background):** The text doesn't say what Elm Quay is, what kinds of cases these are, what prompted the trial, or what the software does and how it was introduced.

**Heading pairs**
- Headline and standfirst share only the name and topic words. The headline says "faster", while the standfirst adds the figures, the scope and the caveat.
- The first subheading shares only the speaker's name with the quotation under it.
- The second subheading shares no words with the first sentence under it.

I found no echo left to report.

*De* and *dem*: *de* is the subject form, *dem* the object form. *Dom* is spoken Swedish and correct only where the text deliberately renders speech.

*Var* and *vart*: *var* is location, *vart* is direction. Similarly *ligga* and *lägga*, *sitta* and *sätta*, *stå* and *ställa* — the first of each pair is intransitive.

*Att* after a modal verb is an error, not a variation: *kan göra*, not *kan att göra*. After *börja*, *sluta*, and *behöva* the bare infinitive is the ordinary form.

Verbs take no person or number marking: *jag är*, *vi är*, *de är*. Adjectives do agree: *ett stort hus*, *stora hus*, *den stora bilen*.

Numbers use a decimal comma and a space as the thousands separator: *3,14*, *1 000 000*. A percentage takes a space before the sign: *50 %*. A range takes an unspaced en dash: *2020–2024*, *sidorna 12–18*.

In running prose a percentage and a degree are written out: *14 procent*, *45 grader*. The sign belongs to technical, statistical, and tabular text, where the temperature degree is spaced as the percentage sign is — *25 °C* — and the angular degree closes up on the number: *90°*.

Dates are written *2026-08-24* or *24 augusti 2026*; month names and weekdays are lowercase, as are nationalities and languages — *svenska*, *måndag*, *en tysk forskare*. Clock times are written *kl. 14.30* or *14:30*; both are current.

Currency follows the amount: *1 250 kr*, *250 000 SEK*, with a space before the unit.

A sentence-initial connective adverb takes no comma before the finite verb: *Dessutom är det viktigt*, not *Dessutom, är det viktigt*.

After a colon, direct speech or a quotation starts with a capital. A closely connected specification or explanation may begin with lowercase even when it is a complete sentence. An unquoted question can similarly stand as an independent utterance with a capital or as an integrated specification with lowercase; both readings can be valid. A colon followed by several sentences takes a capital.

The Swedish dash is the en dash, and it is spaced wherever it stands inside a line: the sentence-breaking dash in *snabbare – det*, and the parenthetical insertion, which takes a space on each side. A dash opening a line takes a space after it and has nothing before it to space against. The range is the exception and is unspaced, as above. Wording inside *”…”* is the speaker's own, and the text vouches for it word for word. A speech dash opens the line, is closed by nothing, and claims the content and the meaning as the speaker's while leaving the wording repairable within the boundary the writing Skill works under: *– Det gick fortare än vi trodde, säger hon.* Repaired wording set inside quotation marks is therefore false about the source rather than a typographic slip. In running prose, *och* is written out: *Service och support*, not *Service & support*. Preserve an ampersand that belongs to a proper name or quoted matter.

Abbreviations take periods: *t.ex.*, *bl.a.*, *dvs.*, *m.m.*, *osv.*, *ca* without one. An initialism compounded with a word takes a hyphen and keeps whichever case it has on its own: *vd-brev*, *USA-baserad*, *EU-direktiv*.

# The mechanics contract

Objective correctness, in the half of it that does not depend on which language a text is in. A Skill contracted to mechanical correction reads this document together with the resolved language's own mechanics guidance, and the two together are that run's rules. What is true of every language the Collection installs is stated here and stated once, so that it is not written again in each language, where the copies would be free to disagree with one another about what is an error.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

Nothing here is a preference. A rule belongs in this document only where the text is wrong whatever the writer intended, and only where it would be wrong in the same way in any language. Spelling, inflection, agreement, the language's own punctuation, and its conventions for dates, numbers, currency, and quotation all turn on the language and belong to that language's resource. Where a language defaults more strictly or more loosely than a rule below, its own guidance says so, and what it says about itself wins.

The examples are English because this document is, and they are patterns rather than strings. Apply each by what it does in the target language rather than by the words it happens to use.

## Clause boundaries

Two independent clauses joined by a comma alone are an error where the second does not explain, specify, restate, or stand in direct contrast to the first. *The project will be expensive, it starts in the spring* puts two statements in one sentence that have nothing to do with each other beyond sitting there together: the reader takes the comma as a signal that the sentence continues, and meets a new subject and a new verb instead. Two clauses run together with no punctuation at the joint at all are the same error, and take the same correction.

The same joint is not an error where the second clause does explain, specify, restate, or contrast with the first. *The bug was not in the parser, it was in a silent retry* is the negative-positive contrast, where the comma is what holds the two halves together as one statement, and separating them would break a single thought into two. *We shipped it anyway, nobody had a better idea* specifies the first clause with the reason behind it. Both are established usage rather than tolerated looseness, and a pass that corrects them has changed how the sentence reads without being asked to.

Judge a joint by whether the clauses cohere, and not by their length, by how formal the text is, or by how the text punctuates elsewhere. Where the reading is genuinely open — where a careful reader could defend the joint — the comma stands, because what this rule reaches is the boundary that misleads and not the boundary that is merely informal.

Correct an erroneous joint at the joint and nowhere else: the comma becomes a period or a semicolon, and nothing else about the sentence moves. Do not reorder the clauses, do not merge them into one, and do not supply a conjunction — *and*, *but*, and *so* each assert a relation between the two clauses, and the writer asserted none. Neither half is rewritten, split, or tightened on the way past. Where more than one of a period and a semicolon would serve, the period is the safer of the two, since it claims nothing about how closely the statements are related.

## Quotation

Quoted matter reaches a reader in one of three settings, and the setting decides what the punctuation and capitalisation around it have to do. A quotation is run into a sentence, set off as a block of its own, or reported as speech, and a reader takes each of the three as a different promise about where the sentence ends, where the source's words begin, and who is speaking. The marks are the language's. Which glyphs enclose a quotation, which side of a closing mark a stop falls on, and how speech is conventionally set are stated in the resolved language's mechanics scope and not here, and the marks in the examples below stand in for whichever ones it names. What follows holds whatever they turn out to be — which setting a quotation is in, and what that setting then requires.

A run-in quotation is part of the sentence carrying it, and the joint between the two is punctuated by what the quoted words do there. Where the quotation is introduced as an utterance of its own, a stop stands at the joint and the quotation opens the way a sentence opens: *She replied, "I'll be there."* Where the quoted words are instead a grammatical part of the host sentence — its object, its complement, a fragment the sentence reads straight through — no stop stands at the joint and the quotation takes the case the surrounding syntax needs: *She called the proposal "completely unacceptable"*, not *She called the proposal, "Completely unacceptable"*. A stop at that joint promises the reader an utterance and then hands them a sentence with no room for one. Which of a comma and a colon introduces an utterance is a matter for the writer and for the language; whether a stop stands at the joint at all is neither.

The sentence around a run-in quotation still ends, and it ends once. A quoted sentence's own final stop and the host sentence's stop are one stop and not two, and where the quoted matter ends in a question or exclamation mark that mark stands alone and takes no comma beside it: *"Will you?" she asked*, not *"Will you?", she asked*. A reporting clause is bound to the utterance it reports rather than being a sentence in its own right, so it takes no capital and never stands behind a full stop: *"I'll come," she said*, not *"I'll come." She said.* Which side of the closing mark the surviving stop falls on is settled by the language and not here.

A block quotation is marked by being set off, and that setting is the whole of the mark. Marks enclosing a block state the quotation a second time, and they cost the reader the one thing the block was doing for them: inside a block, marks are the source's own and are preserved as the source wrote them. Because the block itself takes no level, a quotation inside one stands at the outermost level the language has rather than at the level it would take nested inside another.

The sentence introducing a block has finished by the time the block begins, and the block ends on the quoted matter's own punctuation, so the surrounding sentence's stop does not follow the block and no part of the host sentence is left hanging past it. A source named with a block sits outside the quotation and after it; set inside, the attribution reads as something the source wrote about itself.

Reported speech is punctuated as a run-in quotation is, and what the setting adds is the layout that says who is speaking. A turn belongs to one speaker and takes a paragraph of its own, and a second speaker beginning inside the first speaker's paragraph is read as the first speaker still talking, however plainly the words belong to somebody else. Where one speaker's turn runs across more than one paragraph, the continuation is marked as the same turn, because a reader shown nothing takes the second paragraph for somebody else's turn: a new paragraph is what a change of speaker looks like in this setting. How a language marks the continuation is its own — a turn left unclosed until its last paragraph, a speech mark opening every one of them — but that the reader can tell one continued turn from two is not the language's to settle.

A quotation promises that the words inside it are the source's, and three departures from that promise are each marked where they occur. Words added or altered so that the quotation fits its host sentence — a pronoun resolved, a tense harmonised, an initial capital raised or lowered to suit the surrounding syntax — are marked as the writer's rather than the source's: *"[T]he proposal was unacceptable"*. Words left out are marked at the gap, so that the reader is not shown a continuous sentence the source never wrote: *"the proposal … was unacceptable"*. An error the source made is kept and marked as the source's — *[sic]* — because quoted matter is not the text's own, and an error corrected inside a quotation makes the quotation false about its source. Unmarked, each of the three reads as the source's own words, which is the single thing the reader took the quotation to guarantee.

## Abbreviations spelled out

The capitals in an abbreviation are a property of the abbreviation and say nothing about the words behind it, so a spelled-out form is capitalised the way those same words are capitalised anywhere else in the text. *Search engine optimisation* and *hypertext markup language* are the forms; *Search Engine Optimisation* and *HyperText Markup Language* are the error, and it comes from reading the capitals backwards out of *SEO* and *HTML*. What it does to a reader is assert a name the text does not have: capitals in running prose mark a proper noun, and a reader meeting them takes the words for the title of a product, a standard, or an organisation rather than for a description of what the abbreviation stands for.

Where the words behind an abbreviation are a proper name, they keep the capitals the name has anyway: *North Atlantic Treaty Organization*, *World Health Organization*. That is the name's capitalisation and not the abbreviation's, which is why the abbreviation is no guide to it — *WHO* and *HTML* look alike, and the words behind them are not the same kind of thing. Correct at the spelled-out form and nowhere else: the abbreviation keeps its own capitals, and where and how the text introduces it is untouched.

## Lists

A list holds one convention for punctuation and capitalisation, and holds it in every item. Which convention it can hold follows from what the items are. Items that are complete sentences are punctuated as sentences, capital and terminal stop, because a sentence does not stop being one for sitting in a list; items that are fragments completing the sentence that introduces them are punctuated as parts of that sentence, and a list of fragments therefore has more than one correct treatment. What is wrong in either case is holding two at once, because the reader takes the change as meaning something: the fragment among sentences reads as truncated, and the one item ending in a stop reads as the end of the list.

Correct at the items that depart from the convention the rest of the list keeps, and nowhere else. The stop closing the last item of a list of fragments is the introducing sentence ending rather than a departure from the list's convention, and it stands. Where the items are genuinely of both kinds, what would have to change is an item and not its punctuation, and rewriting an item is past where a mechanical pass stops.

## Established variants

Where a language establishes more than one correct form, the text's own choice stands. A form is not an error because another form is more common, more modern, or the one the reader would have written, and the correction is never to normalise the text towards one of them. Only inconsistency within one text is corrected, and it is corrected towards whichever of the established forms that text already uses more.

That preserves nothing the rules in hand name as an error. A construction this contract or the resolved language's own mechanics guidance identifies as wrong is corrected however consistently the text commits to it, because consistency is what an established variant is judged by and never what makes something established. A text that is wrong the same way throughout is wrong throughout.

Tre fynd står kvar olösta eftersom texten saknar underlaget som skulle behövas. Svaret är målet, så `input.md` är orörd.

```markdown
# Ärenden tilldelades snabbare i Elm Quays försök

**Under ett åtta veckor långt försök med programvara från leverantören Svale registrerade Elm Quay 31 ärenden, akuta ärenden undantagna. Tiden till tilldelning var två arbetsdagar mot tidigare tre, men enligt kundens försöksanteckning kan skillnaden inte tillskrivas programvaran. Läs vad kundens arbetsledare Maya Lind skulle göra annorlunda.**

Elm Quay använde programvara från Svale i ett åtta veckor långt försök. Kundens försöksanteckning visar både utfallet och vad utfallet inte säger, och arbetsledaren Maya Lind på Elm Quay ger sin bedömning.

## Maya Lind bedömer försöket

– Att ha en gemensam bild av ärendena hjälper oss, men jag skulle lägga till en vecka för förberedelser, säger Maya Lind, arbetsledare hos kunden.

## Kortare tilldelningstid kan inte knytas till programvaran

Enligt kundens försöksanteckning registrerades 31 ärenden under åtta veckor, med akuta ärenden undantagna. Tiden till tilldelning var två arbetsdagar jämfört med tre tidigare. Anteckningen säger att arbetsbelastningen var olika och att skillnaden inte kan tillskrivas programvaran.

– Jag skulle välja att göra försöket igen, säger Lind.

Kundcaset publiceras av leverantören Svale.
```

**Olösta fynd**

1. **Byline saknas.** Artikelns anatomi kräver en byline mellan ingressen och brödtexten. Varken texten eller anropet namnger någon författare, så platsen står tom. Det är det enda mätbara krav som fortfarande inte uppfylls.
2. **Uppmaning till handling saknas i avslutningen.** Ett kundcase får bara använda erbjudanden, länkar och kontaktvägar som redan finns, och texten innehåller inga. Läsaren får alltså inget nästa steg.
3. **Genrens luckor.** Texten säger inte vad Elm Quay är, vilka slags ärenden det gäller, vad som ledde till försöket eller vad Svales programvara gör och hur den infördes. Utan det kan läsaren inte bedöma resultatet. Luckorna kan inte fyllas ur texten.

**Strukna påståenden**

- ”Vi på Svale är världsledande på att skapa framgång” i inledningen. Det saknade stöd, och leverantören berättade med sitt eget ”vi”.
- ”kunden stod hjälplös innan vi kom” i inledningen. Det var en räddningsberättelse utan stöd, och resten av texten visar kunden som en part som själv agerar.
- ”Vår programvara orsakade därför hela förbättringen.” Meningen drog en slutsats om orsak som meningen före uttryckligen avvisar. Den meningen, om att arbetsbelastningen var olika och att skillnaden inte kan tillskrivas programvaran, står kvar ordagrant.
- ”räddade” och ”fantastiska” i rubriken, och ”bevisar allt” i den andra underrubriken. Orden påstod mer än texten stöder.
- Bryggan ”Maya Lind säger att det hjälper att ha en gemensam bild av ärendena.” Den upprepade bara citatet. Påståendet står kvar i citatet, och vem som säger det framgår av anföringen.
- ”Elm Quay registrerade 31 ärenden.” ströks ur inledningen eftersom meningen upprepade ingressen. Uppgiften står kvar, med period och undantag, i ingressen och i resultatavsnittet.

**Ändrade påståenden**

- Siffran 31 i ingressen står nu tillsammans med perioden på åtta veckor och undantaget för akuta ärenden.
- Att Elm Quay prövade programvara från Svale i ett försök står nu uttryckligen i ingressen och inledningen. Tidigare framgick det bara indirekt av ”Vår programvara” och sista raden.
- Rubriken säger nu att ärenden tilldelades snabbare. Det bygger på att tiden gick från tre arbetsdagar till två, och rubriken påstår inget orsakssamband.
- Underrubriken ”Kortare tilldelningstid kan inte knytas till programvaran” säger utan källa det som brödtexten tillskriver kundens försöksanteckning. Brödtexten anger fortfarande att det är anteckningen som säger det.

Utöver påståendena ovan skrevs rubriken och båda underrubrikerna om så att de håller sig till textens egen styrka. Den första underrubriken lämnar dessutom poängen åt citatet under den. Den dubblerade ingressen skrevs om till en fristående sammanfattning. Inledningen skrevs om så att den för texten framåt och introducerar försöket och Maya Lind. Reklamspråk och leverantörens eget ”vi” togs bort. Den avslutande mekaniska korrekturläsningen hittade inga fel att rätta.
